claim: Anderson's rational model of categorisation is a Dirichlet-process (Chinese-restaurant) mixture: the number of clusters is set by the data and a coupling parameter c moves it between exemplar-like (many small clusters) and prototype-like (few large clusters). Anderson's original local-MAP search is order-dependent and brittle (second-best cluster can sit at a 0.9997 posterior ratio to the best).
agent_test: In S2 REPRESENT, compare a fixed number of candidate rules against a 'open a new rule only when no existing rule fits' policy on the same example sets at equal tokens; score rule-set size and held-out accuracy.

claim: A single-particle filter (one sampled partition, no revision of the best guess) matches human order effects and non-linearly separable data better than local MAP: 25 of 40 people (62.5%) showed the order effect, single particle 63% of runs, M=100 particles 52%, local MAP 100%; on Smith and Minda data the single particle had higher likelihood in all 80 settings. Fits are correlations on a handful of transfer items.
agent_test: Run the agent's rule induction with one sampled hypothesis path versus many paths at equal tokens, shuffle example order, and measure order sensitivity of the final rule and accuracy.

claim: Category difficulty tracks the number of clusters or rules needed. Shepard, Hovland and Jenkins types order I < II < III-V < VI in people (replicated by Nosofsky 1994, N=120, and Badham 2017, N=96); SUSTAIN needs 2, 4, 6, 8 clusters for I, II, III-V, VI. Anderson's RMC fits this order poorly in the ERMI paper's simulation (Shepard MSE 0.10, type 2 error .34).
agent_test: Give the agent synthetic Shepard-type tasks in words; check that the number of rules it writes grows with type and that tokens spent grow with it.

claim: What is learned depends on the question asked. Inference learning (predict a missing feature) is faster for linear structure (6.5 vs 12.3 blocks); classification is faster for non-linear structure (10.4 vs 27.4 blocks). Learning a name per item beats learning two category labels (7.1 vs 9.7 blocks). SUSTAIN reproduces both; the empirical studies themselves were read only through Love et al. 2004.
agent_test: Present the same example set once as 'predict the label' and once as 'predict the missing feature'; compare rules induced and held-out accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: Early in category learning behaviour looks prototype-like, later exemplar-like: in the Smith and Minda non-linearly separable task (16 people, 10 segments) exceptions are missed in the first 3 segments and fixed from segment 4. Claude-2 prompted directly was fully exemplar-based from block 2, unlike humans and ERMI.
agent_test: Measure whether the agent first writes a general rule then adds exceptions as examples accumulate, versus memorising items; compare to a flat memorise-all baseline at equal tokens.

claim: The mechanism of the prototype-to-exemplar shift is contested: it is explained by a prior favouring simple representations that data overwhelm (HDP; Cobweb with prior strength alpha=2, but alpha<0.6 removes the shift) and, by a rival, by attention changes (Nosofsky and Zaki 2002). The effect appears only with specific parameter settings.
agent_test: None direct; treat the shift as a phenomenon, not as proof of any one model, when designing S7 re-fit rules.

claim: Explanation-based generalisation learns a general rule from one example by proving the example with a domain theory and regressing the goal through the proof. It fails when the theory is incomplete, intractable or inconsistent, and suffers the utility problem (too many learned rules slow search).
agent_test: For tasks with a stated domain theory, compare 'explain one example then generalise' versus 'induce from many examples' at equal tokens; vary theory quality (complete, incomplete, wrong) and count rule-library size effects.

claim: Propose-test-refine loops with an external checker beat direct prompting on rule induction. ARC 100 tasks (GPT-4): direct 17%, program 23%, summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected 33%, human-written 45%. ACRE task accuracy 28% to 59%. Boundary: no gain on MiniARC task accuracy (13.8 baseline vs 14.6 at best; raw falls 33.1 to 18.7), and refinement rescued only 4.3% of wrong hypotheses in the Parab study.
agent_test: At equal tokens, compare direct answer versus N hypotheses written in words, each checked against all examples by code or a separate check, on ARC-like and list-function items.

claim: Hypothesis generation, not program writing, is the main bottleneck: GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 of 100 ARC tasks (of those, 67% gave correct programs); in List Functions the generator was 46.4% correct, the summarizer dropped 26% of correct hypotheses (12.1 points lost), the implementor was 61.2%. With 2025-26 models (FalsifyBench) the first failure is the test step: instruction-tuned models confirm in 66-82% of tests, reasoning models 24-39%, and success is 33-41% vs 68-75% for the top reasoning models.
agent_test: Log per-stage correctness in the agent (hypothesis, filter, apply) on a labelled set; test whether skipping any summarising or pruning step raises recall at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs propose better rules than they can apply: with the LM itself as interpreter, MiniSCAN task accuracy falls from over 80% to about 0, though the drop is smaller elsewhere (ACRE 59.0 to 47.0, List Functions 61.2 to 50.0, MiniARC 14.6 to 5.4; the last three read from Qiu et al. table, inferred mapping).
agent_test: After the agent states a rule, test it on each given example by an explicit step-by-step check and by code; measure how often the in-model check disagrees with the code.

claim: Rule induction by an LLM is brittle to noisy exemplars (1-2 corrupted of 8 hurts clearly, accuracy keeps falling at 12.5, 25 and 50%) and to unfamiliar output vocabulary; a prompt warning only partly helps. Exact accuracies were in figures not transcribed. Confirmed by a second lab (Li et al. 2025): list-function accuracy falls steadily with 10 to 30% noise (GPT-4o 39.9 to 26.1) and even DeepSeek-R1 flips which instances it solves; subset-sampled rules plus execution feedback cut the drop to about 2.8 points.
agent_test: Corrupt 1 of 8 examples in held-out items; compare an agent that must fit every example against one allowed to name exceptions or outliers, at equal tokens.

claim: An LLM proposing 50-100 natural-language hypotheses, re-weighted by a Bayesian prior and likelihood, fits human concept learning: Number Game (original model needed over 5000 hypotheses), logical concepts R2 = .81 with 100 proposals, within 3% of human accuracy. English hypotheses fit better than Python ones. Online updating of such rules explains human Zendo accuracy (fuzzy rules R2 = .57; hard rules .10), although hard rules score higher.
agent_test: Keep 50-100 candidate rules with weights, update weights per new example, compare to keeping one rule; measure accuracy and stability at equal tokens.

claim: In the number game, GPT o1-mini generalises less like humans than a Bayesian model does: mean JSD human-Bayes 0.36 vs GPT-Bayes 0.56; fitted rule bias humans 0.9, GPT 1.0; ablation suggests the LLM behaves like a maximum-likelihood learner (best variant MaxL) while humans fit a prior-plus-averaging variant (BinL 0.33). GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 and LLaMA-3-8B were less structured. Wong et al. also found GPT-4's own ratings differed from humans.
agent_test: Give one-example and four-example number-game style items; compare agent's graded generalisation to a size-principle Bayes model; check that a prompt to weigh smaller consistent hypotheses closes the gap.

claim: A network meta-trained on LLM-generated category tasks (ERMI) fits human category-learning choices as well as or better than seven cognitive models, but not credibly better than RMC on Badham 2017 types 1-4 (posterior frequency .43 vs .41, errors +-.05). Claude-v2 prompted directly fits worse (BIC 39816.90 vs 38722.13; MSE .18 vs .05). ERMI also reaches 70.95% on 23 OpenML tasks vs TabPFN 70.51%.
agent_test: Compare the agent with priors drawn from its own generated example tasks against zero-shot, on small human-style concept tasks, at equal tokens.

claim: Reusing induced knowledge outside the single task helps LLM agents: explanations added to few-shot examples help a 280B model (untuned explanation gain about one third of example gain, 40 tasks); a rule library from induction lifts CLUTRR +11.1 to +16.4 points and GPT-3.5 using GPT-4 rules +27.2; ExpeL insights reach HotpotQA 40% vs Reflexion 39%. Random rules hurt.
agent_test: Store verified rules and their explanations in memory for repeated task families; compare against no memory and against storing raw examples at equal tokens, plus a random-rule control.

claim: Generalisation gradients differ by test format and framing much more than by whether learning was categorical or predictive (preregistered, Exp 1 N=277, Exp 2 N=245; decisions steeper, BF>1000; absolute framing about 20% more Gaussian). Domain interactions did not replicate in the second test phase.
agent_test: Ask the same generalisation probe as ranking, yes/no decision, and rating; check agent answer shape changes with format.

claim: Rule induction by program and direct (transductive) answering solve different ARC problems and combine well: ensemble 26.50%, induction 18.78%, transduction 15.25% (GPT-4 descriptions, validation, 2 tries).
agent_test: At equal tokens, split budget between rule-then-apply and direct answer, then pick by agreement with the examples; compare to spending all on one.

claim: LLMs lag humans on concept abstraction in ConceptARC: humans 91%, GPT-4 zero-shot 25% (one-shot 33%), best ARC program 52%; minimal tasks humans 0.95 vs GPT-4 text 0.69. Models are 2023-era; same research group reports both papers.
agent_test: Run the current agent on ConceptARC minimal tasks as a fixed-effort regression test for S2.

claim: Fine-tuning an LLM on many psychology experiments (Centaur, Psych-101) predicts human choices including Shepard-type categorisation better than cognitive models, but only aggregate fit numbers were read (response-time check conditional R2 .58 vs Llama .40 vs cognitive models .38).
agent_test: None at prompt level; training is out of scope for a scaffold.

claim: A category-utility (maximal mutual information) taxonomy model, Cobweb, fits classic data comparably to RMC: Medin and Schaffer Exp 1 Spearman .95 vs RMC .91 (RMC order similar, footnote), Hayes-Roth .95-.96, Exp 2 nearly equal to the context model (.96). The difference on ~6 items has no test.
agent_test: Have the agent organise examples as a tree of groups, then compare with a flat list of rules for new-item prediction and token cost.

claim: LLMs can cluster by user goal in language: an LLM proposes cluster descriptions, assigns texts, and an integer program picks a small low-overlap set; humans preferred its explanations 80% vs 56% (LDA) and 71% (Instructor). Covers 66% of samples on average.
agent_test: When the agent groups items, make it state each group in words and score coverage and overlap versus unconstrained grouping at equal tokens.

claim: Abstract-rule tasks are easier than statistics-matched metamer tasks for humans, the reverse for neural networks (networks beat humans on metamers in 7 of 8 abstractions).
agent_test: Build rule tasks and metamer controls; check whether the agent solves by stating the rule or by surface pattern.

claim: In LLM rule induction, independently sampled hypotheses are mostly duplicates: among failed list-function instances only 1.40 unique programs in 2 samples, 2.92 in 8 and 7.89 in 32. Prompting for K distinct concepts first, then one hypothesis per concept, gives +4.5 points (GPT-4o-mini) and +5.0 (Llama-3.1-70B) at equal sample count. Pool breadth helps, but only if the candidates are distinct.
agent_test: Run the agent with 8 candidate rules sampled IID vs 8 rules from a 'list distinct concepts first' step on the same ARC or list-function items at equal tokens; count distinct rules and held-out accuracy.

claim: A candidate pool plus execution against all examples beats a single pass on ARC: program sampling 43% (Greenblatt) vs o1-preview 18% and Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14% single pass. Induction and transduction solve different tasks, and a fallback when no rule fits the examples lifted ARC validation from 18.78% to 26.50%. About 9% of rules that fit all training pairs still fail on the test.
agent_test: Add an S7 rule: if no candidate fits all examples, switch to direct answering or a new rule family; count how often a rule that fit all examples still fails held-out items.

claim: Calling for a falsifying test is the main lever with current models: in FalsifyBench, confirmation-bias share is 24-39% for reasoning models vs 66-82% for instruction-tuned, and the two move with success. Failed games drift into partly overlapping rules and surface word features (92-98% of failed games for the top models contained a surface-feature hypothesis).
agent_test: In S7 force one test input chosen to break the current rule (an item inside a broader plausible rule but outside the current one); compare to confirm-only testing.

claim: Executable rule application is the cheap fix for in-model application errors: writing the rule as code and running it gave PAL +15 points absolute over CoT on GSM8K and near-100% accuracy as object counts grew, while Li et al. 2025 get their noise robustness from execution feedback. No measured token cost versus the 59.0 to 47.0 ACRE drop was found.
agent_test: Compare rule applied in prose vs rule as a function run on every example, at equal tokens, on ACRE-style or list-function items; report token cost.

claim: Example order matters for in-context learning (one SST-2 permutation 88.7% to 51.6% when the model changed; near-chance to near state of the art across orders), and majority voting over sampled paths adds +3.9 to +17.9 points on reasoning benchmarks. Neither was measured on 2025-26 reasoning models doing rule induction, so the order effect for LLM rule induction is plausible but unmeasured.
agent_test: Shuffle the example order 5 times, induce a rule each time, vote on held-out items; measure the spread and the gain from voting.

claim: An LLM rule or experience library needs a strict filter: agents copy retrieved records (experience-following), wrong or off-distribution records propagate, deletion by measured later utility helped real agents with a strict evaluator and hurt with a noisy one, cutting memory about 3x. The Minton utility-problem numbers were not read.
agent_test: Keep a success and failure count per stored rule; delete rules that fail when retrieved; compare accuracy and tokens against an add-only library.

claim: The size principle arithmetic is verified: likelihood is (1/size)^n, so after {16,8,2,64} powers of two beats even numbers by nearly 5000:1 (7.7e-4 vs 1.6e-7), and 'powers of two except 32' needs a prior to be rejected. Whether a size-principle prompt moves LLM number-game answers toward humans is untested (Bazigaran 2025 JSD .56 vs best fit .49 is the only measure).
agent_test: In S2 ask the agent to list all consistent rules and prefer the one allowing the fewest other cases; test on number-game items against human ratings.
